title: Hymnsong Records
subject: Constitutional Law
stem:
Hymnsong Records Inc. is a Tennessee corporation that produces Christian-music albums. It wants to distribute its catalog in California. California requires out-of-state recording companies to pay an annual distribution license fee of $3,200, while California-incorporated recording companies pay $1,400. Hymnsong sues California in federal court, asserting only an Article IV Privileges and Immunities claim against the higher fee.

What is California's strongest response to that claim?
call: What is California's strongest response to that claim?

choices.A: Hymnsong is not a citizen for Article IV Privileges and Immunities purposes.
choices.B: Article IV Privileges and Immunities protects corporations whenever they distribute across state lines.
choices.C: Hymnsong wins automatically because the higher fee is a fundamental burden on out-of-state commerce.
choices.D: Article IV Privileges and Immunities applies only to criminal defendants.

rightExplanation: California's strongest response is A. Article IV, Section 2, of the Constitution (the "Comity Clause") protects only the "Citizens of the several States" — that is, natural persons who are citizens of a state other than the forum state. A corporation, even one incorporated in another state, is not a "citizen" for Article IV P&I purposes; corporations must look to other doctrines (e.g., the dormant Commerce Clause, the Privileges or Immunities Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, or Equal Protection) to challenge discriminatory state regulation. Gold Key: the Article IV P&I plaintiff threshold is a person-class threshold, not a burdens-on-commerce threshold — and a corporation is not in the protected class at all.

c3.label: CUT
c3.text:
- B ("Article IV P&I protects corporations whenever they distribute across state lines") is cut by the Gold Key (person-class threshold): the clause's text and case law require a natural-person citizen of another state; a corporation is not in the protected class. The "whenever" overclaim is the mold's signature.
- C ("Hymnsong wins automatically because the higher fee is a fundamental burden on out-of-state commerce") is cut by the same Gold Key: the person-class objection resolves the case before any merits-level "fundamental burden" theory is reached. The "automatically" is a tiered-absolute overclaim.
- D ("Article IV P&I applies only to criminal defendants") is cut by a Call to black-letter law: Article IV P&I protects civil economic rights of natural citizen-plaintiffs (e.g., United Building & Construction Trades Council v. Mayor of Camden, 465 U.S. 208 (1984)) and is not limited to criminal matters. The "criminal-only" frame is a flat misstatement.

c3.label: CLASH / CALL
c3.text: B, C, and D are all eliminated at the person-class threshold (A) — the person-class objection is dispositive. There is no surviving CLASH. The Gold Key resolves the residue: Hymnsong loses because it is not a citizen for Article IV P&I. Residual answer: A.

studentScript: Step 1 — person-class. Article IV P&I protects only natural-person citizens of other states. Hymnsong is a corporation. Gold Key: the case is resolved at the threshold; the merits are never reached. Step 2 — distractors. B bridges from 'interstate burden' to 'Article IV applies' — the bridge is wrong. C asserts an automatic merits win — the merits never get reached. D limits Article IV to criminal defendants — wrong; Article IV P&I protects civil economic rights of natural citizens. Choose A.

A.signal: This is the only answer that engages the Article IV P&I person-class threshold; it disposes of the case before the merits.
A.lawyer: Article IV P&I protects only the 'Citizens of each State,' i.e., natural persons; a corporation is not a citizen and cannot invoke the clause. Paul v. Virginia, 75 U.S. (8 Wall.) 168 (1869).

B.signal: The student bridges from 'interstate burden' to 'Article IV must apply.' The Gold Key rejects the bridge: a corporation is outside the protected class.
B.lawyer: Article IV P&I does not protect corporations; the dormant Commerce Clause addresses the interstate-burden argument, but Hymnsong did not plead that doctrine.

C.signal: The student skips the person-class threshold and asserts automatic victory on a 'fundamental burden' theory. The Gold Key blocks the merits entirely.
C.lawyer: Even if a higher fee burdened out-of-state commerce, Article IV P&I does not reach a corporate plaintiff; the case is dismissed at the threshold, not on the merits.

D.signal: The student conflates Article IV P&I with the Sixth Amendment's criminal-procedure rights. Article IV P&I protects civil economic rights of natural citizen-plaintiffs.
D.lawyer: Article IV P&I is a clause about civil economic and fundamental rights of natural citizens (e.g., right to practice a livelihood, right to own property), not a criminal-procedure clause. See United Building & Construction Trades Council v. Mayor of Camden, 465 U.S. 208 (1984).

goldKeys.statement: Article IV Privileges and Immunities protects only the natural-person citizens of other states. A corporation is not a citizen for that clause, so a corporate plaintiff cannot use Article IV P&I to challenge a state's higher regulatory fee.
goldKeys.trigger: out-of-state non-natural-person entity challenges a higher state fee under Article IV P&I
goldKeys.unlocks: interstate-burden bridge trap (B) and tiered-absolute automatic-win trap (C)
goldKeys.authority: Article IV, Section 2, U.S. Constitution; Paul v. Virginia, 75 U.S. (8 Wall.) 168 (1869); United Building & Construction Trades Council v. Mayor of Camden, 465 U.S. 208 (1984)

remediation.title: Article IV P&I person-class threshold
remediation.signal: A non-natural-person entity (corporation, LLC, partnership) sues under only Article IV Privileges and Immunities.
remediation.studentMove: Cut the merits. The clause's text and case law require a natural-person citizen of another state; a corporation is not a citizen. The case is resolved at the threshold.
remediation.tinyRule: Article IV P&I protects only natural-person citizens of other states.
remediation.trap: The student bridges from 'interstate burden' to 'Article IV applies' or jumps to a 'fundamental burden' merits theory. Both miss the person-class threshold.
